definition: 'AI tiger' (Chinese: AI六小虎, romanized: AI liù xiǎohǔ, lit.
details: 'Six AI little tigers') is a term for notable startup companies in the artificial intelligence industry in China. There are commonly six companies defined as AI tigers: Z.ai (GLM), Moonshot AI (Kimi), MiniMax, Baichuan, StepFun, and 01.AI. Funding rounds for the tigers are led by BATX, which are composed of China's four largest tech firms.

explainer.lead: AI tiger is a collective nickname for six notable Chinese AI startups, not a company or model. The label is useful when discussing China's AI industry, its funding, and how its startups compare with much larger US laboratories.

tiers.eli5: Imagine giving one team name to six promising new companies so you can talk about them together. That is what AI tiger does for six Chinese companies building AI, including the makers of GLM and Kimi. The nickname does not mean they all make the same thing or have the same amount of money.
tiers.practitioner: Treat AI tiger as an ecosystem label rather than a technical category or guarantee of model capability. It can help identify companies such as Z.ai, Moonshot AI, and StepFun when comparing Chinese AI providers; StepFun, for example, emphasizes multimodal models with text and video input. Funding context also matters: Aylon Berger argues that these startups are more capital-constrained than frontier US laboratories, while investment restrictions on both sides hinder US-China AI deals.
tiers.paperLevel: The commonly used set is AI tigers = {Z.ai (GLM), Moonshot AI (Kimi), MiniMax, Baichuan, StepFun, 01.AI}, denoting notable Chinese AI startups. Aylon Berger of the Lowy Institute identifies relative financial-capital constraints and US and Chinese investment controls as limits on the group. Z.ai's US$558 million Hong Kong IPO on 8 January 2026 and MiniMax's $620 million IPO on 9 January were contrasted with valuations of $500 billion for OpenAI and $183 billion for Anthropic.

explainer.example: If an article calls Moonshot AI an AI tiger, it means that the company behind Kimi belongs to this commonly named six-company group. It does not mean that Kimi itself is an AI tiger or that Moonshot AI shares a model with the other five companies.

explainer.intuition: The term bundles six startups into one recognizable group, much like a nickname for a cohort of companies. It describes their place in China's AI industry rather than a shared architecture or technical method.
howItWorks: Identify the six companies commonly included: Z.ai, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, Baichuan, StepFun, and 01.AI.
Use the shared label when discussing them collectively as Chinese AI startups.
Keep their individual work distinct, such as Z.ai's GLM, Moonshot AI's Kimi, and StepFun's multimodal focus.
Consider their funding context, including rounds led by BATX, China's four largest tech firms.
explainer.whyItMatters: The label provides a compact way to compare an important group of Chinese startups and examine their financing and constraints. Berger's comparison highlights a large capital gap with frontier US laboratories, alongside restrictions that stifle US-China AI investment deals.
misconceptions: An AI tiger is not a single AI model, product, or company.
BATX is not another tiger; it refers to China's four largest tech firms, which lead funding rounds for the group.
Membership in the group does not imply identical technical approaches, as StepFun's text-and-video multimodal focus illustrates.
